analysis.one_liner: Lets workers opt out of Social Security and put their payroll taxes into private tax-exempt retirement accounts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors on December 19, 2018 — fifteen days before the Congress ended — the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any worker elect to leave Social Security's retirement and disability system. The worker's 6.2% payroll tax would instead be deposited into a personal, tax-exempt "S.A.F.E. account" held by a bank or approved trustee, with the employer's matching share added starting in the sixteenth year. In exchange, the electing worker would receive no Social Security retirement, disability, survivor, or family benefits — only whatever the account holds — while Medicare hospital insurance would be unaffected.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who elect out and whose investments do well would own an account that grows tax-free and can be passed to heirs, unlike a Social Security benefit that ends at death. Banks and financial firms would gain a new, steady channel of payroll contributions into accounts they are paid to manage. Insurance companies would gain a tax-advantaged channel, since account money could be withdrawn tax-free to buy term life, disability, and long-term care policies.

how_it_helps.text: A worker who elects out stops paying the 6.2% employee Social Security tax and has it deposited instead into a personal S.A.F.E. account; the employer's matching 6.2% is added beginning in the sixteenth year of the election.

The account is tax-exempt: contributions are deductible in arriving at adjusted gross income, earnings grow untaxed, and distributions after age 59½ or on death are tax-free — unlike a Social Security benefit, the balance can be left to heirs.
Money in the account can be withdrawn tax-free before retirement age to pay premiums for long-term care insurance, disability insurance, and term life insurance.
Electing workers keep Medicare hospital insurance: the bill says Medicare entitlement determinations are made without regard to the election.
Participation is voluntary, and a worker can revoke the election during a two-year grace period (though a late revocation cuts the worker's remaining Social Security benefit formula by 20%).

analysis.who_pays: Workers who elect out trade a guaranteed, inflation-adjusted monthly benefit for life — plus disability coverage and benefits for their survivors and dependents — for an account whose value depends on markets, fees, and how long they live; if the account runs out, the income stops. Social Security's trust funds would lose the payroll tax of every elector. Employers must build and run payroll deduction programs at their own expense, facing civil penalties of up to $500,000 for failures.

drawbacks.text: Electing workers lose guaranteed monthly Social Security retirement, disability, survivor, and dependent benefits entirely — the bill bars any monthly benefit payments based on an elector's wages — so a worker whose account performs poorly, becomes disabled, or dies young leaves family members with only what is in the account.
An electing worker bears market risk with no guaranteed floor: the bill provides no annuity, no inflation protection, and no minimum benefit, only the account balance.

Early withdrawals before age 59½ are taxed as income plus an additional 20% tax, and revoking the election after the 90-day window but within two years permanently cuts the worker's Social Security benefit formula by 20%.

Every elector's payroll tax stops flowing into the Social Security trust funds, which are financed by current workers' contributions — the more workers elect out, the tighter the system becomes for those who stay in.
Employers get no compensation for administering the required payroll deduction programs and face civil penalties of up to $500,000 per failure to deduct or to deposit funds on time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker with steady market returns and no need for disability or survivor protection, a personal account that can be inherited has real appeal. But the bill asks workers to give up the parts of Social Security that are hardest to replace privately — disability insurance and lifetime, inflation-protected benefits for widows, widowers, and children — while the employer contribution doesn't even start for fifteen years. The heaviest costs fall on workers who elect and later need the protections they gave up, and the reliable winner under the design is the financial industry that would manage the accounts.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 19, 2018 with no cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means and Oversight committees, and neither committee acted before the Congress ended fifteen days later.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on December 19, 2018, near the end of the 115th Congress.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred that day to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
No hearing, markup, floor action, or vote ever occurred; the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social Security's guaranteed structure — retirement, disability, and survivor benefits — was left untouched. Financial firms did not gain the new account-management channel, and workers never faced the choice of trading guaranteed benefits for market risk.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill drew a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill requires every S.A.F.E. account to be held by a bank or an approved trustee, routing the 6.2% payroll contribution of every electing worker into accounts the financial industry is paid to manage — a permanent new revenue channel. Workers who elect get ownership and tax-free growth, but pay management fees and bear market risk in place of a guaranteed benefit.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: Account holders may withdraw money tax-free before retirement age specifically to buy long-term care, disability, and term life insurance, giving insurers a tax-advantaged sales channel into workers' retirement savings. While the bill bars the account itself from investing in life insurance contracts, it steers electing workers toward purchasing insurers' products with pre-tax money.

Covered employers must set up and run payroll deduction programs at their own expense — the bill bars them from recouping administrative costs — and face civil penalties of up to $500,000 for failing to deduct or deposit funds on time.

industries.industry: Social Security system and its beneficiaries
industries.note: Every electing worker's payroll tax stops flowing into the trust funds that pay current beneficiaries, while the elector themselves forfeits all retirement, disability, survivor, and dependent benefits. Medicare hospital insurance entitlement is expressly preserved.
